turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, both of you. I'm Dr Hale. What brings you in today, Marcus?

[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, I'm fine, honestly. I told Priya we didn't need to use up an appointment. I'm sleeping a bit ordinary and I'm tired, but that's just life, you know, after everything.
[SEG0003] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's not fine. That's why I booked it. He hasn't been himself since the redundancy.

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, okay, I'm not sparkling, I'll give you that. But I don't want to make a big drama out of it. I can still get up, I can still make a cuppa, I'm not falling apart in the street or anything.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): I hear you. There's no drama required. Priya, what have you been noticing at home?

[SEG0006] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He lies awake half the night. Some nights he's still staring at the ceiling at two. And he doesn't want to do anything — not the footy, not seeing his mates, not even the garden, and he used to live out there.

[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): The garden thing is a bit unfair. The mower's been playing up, the catcher's split, and I was going to take it to the bloke in Reservoir but then I thought, what's the point if I'm not even working, and then the weeks just... anyway. I do go out there. Sometimes.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sounds like the get-up-and-go has gone a bit flat. How long has the sleep been like this?
[SEG0009] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Three months. Since the job actually finished.

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No, hang on. The finish date was the end of January, but they gave me notice back in November, and that's when I started waking up stupidly early, so if you're counting properly it's closer to five months, not three. I remember because the Melbourne Cup was on the telly in the break room the week they told us, and I didn't even care who won, which is not like me.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so somewhere between about three and five months, and you're not quite landing on the same start. What does a typical night look like now?

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): I get into bed around eleven, sometimes half past, and I just lie there going over the roster I don't even have, what I should've said in the meeting, whether the payout was right. I might drop off around one, then I'm awake again at four, wide awake, and I don't get back. It's not every single night, maybe five nights a week. The other two I crash and sleep through, which almost makes the next day worse because I've got no routine.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): And in the daytime, energy-wise?

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat, like someone's pulled the plug out. I can do a small thing, like put a load of washing on, and then I need to sit down for ages — it's not sore muscles, I'm not crook that way, there's just no fuel. Coffee doesn't touch it, and I have two in the morning, sometimes a third if Priya's made a pot.
[SEG0015] person_3 (CAREGIVER): And he used to be the one dragging me out for a walk after tea. Now he says he's too buggered.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about interest in things you used to like? You mentioned the footy.

[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I support the Doggies, membership since I was twenty-two, and this season I haven't watched a full game — Priya puts it on and I just look at my phone. It's not that I'm angry at the club, I just don't care. Same with cooking: I used to do a big curry on Sundays, toast the spices and all that, and now we do toast or whatever's in the fridge. I still eat, it's not that I'm not hungry, I just can't be bothered and it doesn't taste like anything special.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the appetite itself is still there, it's the enjoyment and the effort that's gone.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Exactly. I'm not losing weight that I've noticed. Pants fit the same.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. And Marcus, I do need to ask something straight, gently. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or of not wanting to be here?

[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No, definitely not — I've felt useless, and I've thought the whole situation is rubbish, but I have not thought about hurting myself and I don't want to die. I'd tell Priya if that changed, and I know that's the line you're meant to say, but I mean it.
[SEG0022] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He's said that to me too. I've been watching for it. I haven't heard anything like that.

[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you, both of you. That matters, and I believe you. If it ever shifts, you don't sit on it — you ring us or go to emergency. How have you been feeling in yourself, mood-wise, day to day?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Not crying, I don't really do that. It's more grey, like the volume's down on everything. Some arvos I feel a bit irritable with Priya over nothing, the dishwasher or whatever, and then I feel rotten about it. It's not all day every day — mornings are the worst, and by the afternoon I can hold a conversation.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with concentration, reading, that sort of thing?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, actually, um, I started a library book, a big one about the Antarctic, and I've read the same chapter three times and I couldn't tell you what happened. Forms for Centrelink I had to get Priya to check because I kept missing boxes.
[SEG0027] person_3 (CAREGIVER): The Centrelink thing took us two nights. He was never like that with paperwork. He ran a shift of twelve people.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Warehouse supervisor, afternoon shift, at the distribution centre in Laverton, fourteen years. Redundant, not sacked — I want that clear. The site's still there, they just automated half the floor.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a big chunk of your week gone, and your identity with it, by the sound of it. Are you working at all now, or looking?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Not working. I've looked at a few things online and then closed the laptop — I tell myself I'll do applications on Monday and Monday comes and I don't. It's not that I don't want a job, I do, I just can't get the engine to turn over.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Have you ever had a stretch like this before, or any treatment for your mood?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. I've been to the GP for a crook knee years ago and that's about it. No counsellor, no psychologist, nothing like that. My knee settled with physio, I didn't even need an operation.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): And medicines at the moment? Anything from the chemist, even for sleep?

[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): I bought Restavit, the doxylamine one, twenty-five milligrams, and I took it maybe four nights spread over a couple of weeks — not in a row — and I was a zombie till lunchtime, so I stopped back in February. Nothing since, and no antidepressants, I've never been on those. Priya's on something for her blood pressure but that's hers, not mine.
[SEG0035] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I did suggest he try the Restavit again on a smaller dose but he wouldn't.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Because it made the next day worse. I'm not taking it.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Fair enough, we'll leave that one stopped. Did anyone do bloods when this started, or recently?

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, my usual GP, Dr Okonkwo, back when I first went in about the tiredness. I can't tell you the date — um, sometime after New Year, I think January, but don't hold me to that. They said the vitamin D was borderline, not deficient, just borderline, and they didn't give me a number, just to get a bit more sun. Thyroid they said was okay, I think, but I never saw the printout.

[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a borderline vitamin D on their say-so, no figure, and you're not sure of the date. We won't treat that as a hard result. I wouldn't start a tablet for your mood today anyway.

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Good, because I don't want to be on something that changes my personality. I've read all the forums, people saying the first two weeks are rough with nausea and then maybe it helps, and I don't know if I'm bad enough. If you told me to take sertraline tomorrow I don't think I'd fill it, not yet.

[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not prescribing sertraline or anything else today. If the sleep and the flatness are still running the show when I see you next, we can talk properly about whether a medicine is worth it. No decision now.
[SEG0042] person_3 (CAREGIVER): What can we actually do in the meantime? Because I'm running out of ways to coax him.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): A few ordinary things, nothing magic: same wake-up time every day even after a rotten night, and get outside in the morning light for ten or fifteen minutes. Keep the Restavit in the cupboard, and cut the third coffee if you can, especially after lunch. And one small thing a day that used to matter — even half a footy quarter, or five minutes in the garden — not to perform, just to see if a bit of interest comes back.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I can try the morning light — the garden's complicated with the mower, but I could walk to the end of the street, we live in a unit in Coburg so it's not a hike. I don't drink, by the way, if that's the next question; never really have, maybe a beer at Christmas. And I don't smoke.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Good to know. I wasn't about to lecture you. Priya, anything else that's worrying you that we haven't touched?
[SEG0046] person_3 (CAREGIVER): He naps in the afternoon sometimes, an hour, and then of course the night's worse. And he keeps apologising to me, which is sweet and also exhausting.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): The naps are only if I've been up since four, and it's not every day, maybe twice a week. I know it wrecks the night, and I've told myself to stop.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can swap the nap for a short walk, that usually serves you better. I'm not going to order fresh bloods today. If you're no better in a fortnight we can repeat the vitamin D then, properly, and revisit the medicine conversation.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): A fortnight's fine. Should I bring the old results if I can find them? They might be on the My Health Record thing. I'm not great with the login.

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you can get the printout or a screenshot, bring it, but don't lose sleep over the login. We'll cope either way. I'd like to see you again in a fortnight, both of you if Priya can come. Sooner if the dark thoughts show up, which you've been clear they haven't.
[SEG0051] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him here. And I'll try not to talk over him next time.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): You can talk — you notice stuff I explain away. I do want to say I'm not lazy, even if it looks like I'm sitting around. Fourteen years I didn't take a sick day unless I had gastro, and this is different and I hate it.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nobody in this room thinks you're lazy. What I'm hearing is a low mood that's settled in after the redundancy — poor sleep, no fuel, and the things you cared about have gone quiet. I'm not putting a firm label on it today, but that's the shape of it.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. That's fair. More fair than I'm fine, which was me being an idiot at the start.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): You weren't an idiot. You came in, that's the bit that counts. Reception can book the fortnight when you head out. Any questions before you go?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Just — if I have one decent week, do I still come back? Because I'll convince myself I'm sorted and cancel.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Still come. One decent week doesn't close it. I'll see you in a fortnight regardless.

spec.situation: Adult with poor sleep, low energy and loss of interest for months after a job loss or bereavement; partner or parent speaks for them; patient says 'I'm fine' then partly opens up; denies thoughts of self-harm clearly (doctor asks gently); medication discussed but not started today.
features: doctor_misses_topics: the doctor does not ask about everything; topics never discussed are simply absent (no invented denials, no allergy line if allergies were never mentioned).
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

omissions.text: Patient denied wanting to die / not wanting to be here, in addition to denying self-harm thoughts.

Sleep problem includes prolonged sleep-onset insomnia, typically not falling asleep until around 1 am after going to bed around 11 to 11:30 pm, with rumination about the redundancy/payout/meeting; not just waking at 4 am.
Low energy is severe enough that after small tasks like putting on a load of washing he needs to sit down for ages; coffee does not help.
Loss of interest/anhedonia specifically includes not watching full Western Bulldogs games, losing interest in cooking, and food no longer tasting special despite preserved appetite.
Patient reports no enjoyment from food rather than only preserved appetite.
Previous non-psychiatric history: past crook knee that settled with physiotherapy.
Restavit/doxylamine caused significant next-day sedation: 'zombie till lunchtime,' which is why he stopped and refused to retry it.
Doctor specifically said no fresh blood tests would be ordered today.
Follow-up should be in a fortnight and sooner if dark thoughts develop; doctor also asked that Priya attend if possible and advised to still come even if he has one decent week.
